body: It came at supper, face-up on the counter by the bread box between the cheese grater and the *Vindicator*, and he got to it before Gina did and answered it under the table with his thumb: *tell her yes.*

At twenty past eleven the house is in bed and the RAZR goes off in his hand in the dark kitchen, where he has been standing at the open refrigerator for no reason. He takes it to the top of the basement stairs, where it gets its two bars, and answers it there, and carries it down with him. At the bottom he pulls the string on the bulb. Gina’s chair is at the Dell where she left it. He turns it on the concrete so its back is to the furnace, and sits.
“Hi,” Skye says. “I’m on my mother’s balcony with a blanket and a glass of her wine, and you’re in trouble.”
Behind her, through glass, a bird says *momager*.
“The parrot,” she says. “My mother’s inside on the other line with the network. She’s always on with the network. Pasadena. Friday. You said seventy.”
“It was close.”
“It was *not* seventy. I asked a man who was there. He was wearing a fleece, Jack. A *fleece*. I’m docking you a point.”
“From a seven.”
“You’re a six. Sixes don’t get to argue.”
The blanket moves; a chair creaks out on the balcony. “So. News. My people want lunch.”
“Your people.”

“My mother — Debbie, she manages me — and Corinne, who’s my publicist, which means she manages the managing. Sunday. In town. I’ll get you after your church.” She takes a drink. “They want to see you before anybody sees you.”
“Who’s going to see me?”

“Everybody, in February, if Corinne gets her way. There’s a plan. There’s a carpet. The two of us get *spotted* going into something, by a man from a magazine who just happens to be standing right there.” A sound into the glass, half a laugh and half the other thing. “I’m mortified. I’m having a wonderful time. Wear the blazer from the rain.”
“It’s my only blazer.”
“That’s why it’s the one. And I’m driving up Thursday, back into Sol’s. The heater’s broken. Sol says it’s character.” The chair again. “Now. Rehearsal.”
Her voice goes clipped and quick — a woman walking between two meetings with a phone at each ear. “Where’s Youngstown?”
“Ohio.”
“Is Ohio a *choice*?”

He laughs, and she’s already gone on. “That’s Corinne. Corinne will Google you before the bread comes. Now my mother.” A breath, and somebody else comes up out of it: warm as a hotel lobby, younger than it ought to be, a hand on your arm in every word. “Jack. *Jack.* Sit, sit, sit. Are your people *in* something?”
“My father’s on a list at the union hall.”
“Is that a *network*?” And she’s herself again, fast. “Notes. Don’t say *ma’am*, she’s thirty-nine on paper. Don’t look at the bread. She’ll think you’re poor. You are poor. Don’t look at the bread.”
“I won’t look at the bread.”

“Here’s the table.” The chair scrapes; she’s sitting forward. “Corinne wants a story she can control. She doesn’t care if it’s a good one, she cares if it holds still. My mother wants to be liked more than she wants to like you, so let her — it costs you nothing, and she’ll think it was her idea. And the two of them, all through lunch, through the bread and the little spoons, are going to be trying to find out one thing.”
“What.”
“What you want from me.”
The Dell’s dark screen gives him back a guy under a bare bulb who is going to have to answer that over soup.
“Also,” Skye says, “I read your Matthew.”
“My Matthew.”

“You said your grandmother’s tree comes down after the Epiphany. So on Sunday I looked it up on my phone, in a Coffee Bean on Ventura, next to a man writing a screenplay about a dolphin. And Herod is a showrunner. A jealous one. He hears there’s a new lead in town, and he calls the visitors in *secretly* — it says secretly — and he wants the exact date the star showed up. He’s doing the schedule. And then it’s, go find the kid, tell me where he’s shooting, so I can come and *pay my respects*.”
“That’s not —”

“The Magi are the first fans. They see one star and cross a desert with presents for a kid they’ve never met. And then they get a dream and go home by another way.” The glass, the blanket. “That’s a publicist’s move, Jack. They ducked the press.”

He sits forward in Gina’s chair with his elbows on his knees. “They weren’t supposed to be in it,” he says. “That’s the thing about them. No covenant, no prophets, no promises. Foreigners with a star chart. They came anyway. The Church keeps a day for them — for everybody who shows up from outside the story.”
The balcony chair creaks. “That’s good,” Skye says. “That’s annoyingly good. I’m going to have to come to one of these.”
“One of what?”
“Your day for the people from outside.” A sip. “Who picked February?”
“What?”
“That’s my question. In these stories nobody asks who picks the date. They just *run*.”
He hears the foot of the glass touch down on the concrete out there.

“I hate it,” she says. “The carpet. The man from the magazine who happens to be there. You in the blazer, looking kidnapped. I’ve never decided one thing about my own face.” The blanket. “I’d like to be the one who tells people about you.”
Over his head somebody crosses the kitchen in socks for a glass of water, and runs the tap, and goes back up.
When she comes back she’s lower, closer to the phone. “I’m not saying anything else tonight. My mother’s on the other side of a sliding door and you’re on a payment plan.”
“Since when?”
“Since the furnace. Saturday. After I pick you up — which I am.”
“I’ve got a thing at nine. My roommate’s people.”
“Ted’s thing.”
“Ted’s thing.”
“Then I have you from the airport to Ted’s thing.” She counts it off, seven fifty-two to nine. “An hour. I’ve done whole episodes in less.”

Behind her the sliding door opens on a woman’s voice — *no, Tuesday’s fine, Tuesday’s perfect* — and shuts on it, and the parrot gets its word in.
“I believe it,” she says.
At two minutes to midnight, still down there:

A breath, and the hotel lobby is back. “Your Holiness. *Your Holiness.* Sit, sit. Love the hat. Who does your hats? Is that *custom*? Because I know a girl —” and Debbie Callender goes on to ask the Vicar of Christ who handles his representation, and whether he has ever considered a softer white.

body.text: Ten after eleven, the back bedroom. He’s sitting on his own bed with *The Moviegoer* on his knee for a desk and a sheet of Gina’s lined paper on it, writing his brother back, and the first line is already down: *Neither. She can see fine.* The second line has taken him twenty minutes so far.

Ten after eleven, the back bedroom. He’s sitting on his own bed with *The Moviegoer* on his knee for a desk and a sheet of Gina’s lined paper on it, writing his brother back, and the first line is already down: *She’s nearsighted. I’m working fast.* The second line has taken him twenty minutes so far.

Ten after eleven, the back bedroom. He’s sitting on his own bed with *The Moviegoer* on his knee for a desk and a sheet of Gina’s lined paper on it, writing his brother back, and the first line is already down: *She’s not blind, Dan. She sees me.* The second line has taken him twenty minutes so far.

Ten after eleven, the back bedroom. Danny’s letter is folded in thirds inside *The Moviegoer* on the nightstand, waiting for Marisol. On his knee, on a sheet of Gina’s lined paper, he’s writing a thank-you to Rosie for the drawing she’s going to give him at the door on Saturday. He knows about the drawing. She told him it’s a secret.

body: The radiator under the window knocks and ticks. Across the room the parka is folded on Danny’s bed, under the shelf with the one-armed trophy, and the lamp on the nightstand makes a circle that holds the paper and his hand and leaves the rest to the alley light coming through the blind.
At sixteen past, the RAZR goes off beside the lamp. On the outer screen, the little envelope, and the picture icon beside it.

choices.key: The night Danny’s letter came, Skye sent a picture. You opened it and answered it.
response: He opens it.
It comes up small and dim and, at first, wrong — two of her, one laid over the other, a pale girl and a paler one with the dark coming through her. He tilts it to the lamp, and they come apart.

It’s her window, at night. Behind her the room is lit — the lamp, the string of Christmas lights with half of them out — and in front of her the glass has gone black and gives her back to herself. She’s kneeling up on the mattress under it with the white phone raised to her eye like a viewfinder, and she has nothing on. The light is all behind her, so what the window keeps of her is mostly edge: gold along one shoulder and down the long line of her side to the hip, her hair loose over the other shoulder and lit through. The rest is shadow and glass, and through the glass, through her, the beach in the dark and one white line of surf breaking low across her, where the window gives up and lets the outside in. Her chin is up. Her mouth is set. Her eyes are past her own reflection, out on the black — on Del Playa, on the Pacific — daring it to look.
He holds it in the lamplight till the screen dims to save itself, and wakes it, and answers her with the pen still in his other hand.

body: Upstairs, the lamp off. The alley light comes through the blind in stripes and lies across the parka on Danny’s bed. Down the hall his father snores in two parts. He’s on his own bed in his clothes with the RAZR open over his face, and he goes into the Pictures folder and starts from the first one.
The trailer mirror at five in the morning. The hotel-bathroom mirror. The forty buttons. His own shirt in the back of a town car. The bedroom door at first light. The white tree.
The ocean, and the 10 on her hip.

body.text: One more at the bottom of the list, still shut. He leaves it for Saturday.

body: He goes back up to the top and through them again, slower. A girl three time zones away has been holding a phone up to mirrors since the first week of December so a guy in a snow globe would have something to look at. The same girl docked him a point for Pasadena on the word of a man in a fleece. She read Matthew in a Coffee Bean so she could tell him Herod was a showrunner. Tomorrow night at 7:52 she is going to be at an airport in Santa Barbara, with an hour of him before Ted’s thing already counted. Somewhere around the town car he stops being a man lying in his brother’s room who got off the phone first, and he decides it — he can feel himself do it, like setting his feet before a lift — that he’s lucky. That he is, after all, a lucky man.
He’s smiling. At a screen the size of a stamp, in the dark. He puts the back of his wrist against his mouth like that’s going to do anything about it.
“Skye,” he tells the ceiling, which has heard worse from this bed.

He opens a new message and types what they do: *sat 7:52. if theres no marching band im getting back on the plane*. It’s good. It’s their usual. He looks at it, and takes it back out a letter at a time, and lies there with the empty box and the cursor going.
